sections.title: The Attitude Toward Fruit Trees
sections.html:
Fruit trees have special importance, and whoever plants fruit trees in order to add food to the world becomes a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the creation of the world and its sustenance, as it is stated (Bereshit 2:8): "And the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden." Therefore Israel too, when they enter the Land, must cleave to the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He, and plant fruit trees, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:23): "And when you come into the land and plant all manner of trees for food" (Vayikra Rabba 25:3). Planting fruit trees is included in the mitzva of settling the Land (Ḥatam Sofer, Sukka 36a). In our days, it is the farmers who plant orchards who chiefly merit this mitzva, since the benefit of planting fruit trees in private gardens is meagre compared with the fruit grown in orchards for the multitudes of the House of Israel.

A person is compared to a fruit tree, as it is stated (Devarim 20:19): "For man is a tree of the field." Unlike bushes, which grow quickly and reach their peak in a short time, trees grow slowly, and only after they reach maturity do they bear fruit. So too a person: his process of development is slow relative to the other living creatures, and only after he reaches maturity can he bear fruit and become a partner in sustaining and developing the world. In fruit trees the idealistic aim is more evident: they are generally less beautiful, but they do not grow for their own sake; rather, their aim is to bear fruit in order to nourish people and animals with it. The refined person too should strive to resemble a fruit tree, and to bestow of his goodness on his surroundings and his society, and not to care for himself alone.

The Holy One, blessed be He, too taught us to treat fruit trees with respect, for even for the building of the Mishkan He commanded that shittim wood be brought, which are non-fruit-bearing trees, in order to teach us how careful one must be about uprooting fruit trees (Shemot Rabba 35:2; Tanḥuma Vayakhel 9).

The general prohibition of "bal tashḥit" (do not destroy) is learned from the prohibition of destroying fruit trees, for the fruit tree is the clearest example of something of value, since it is a source of blessing from which grow fruits that give life and joy. Therefore the Sages said that when a fruit tree is uprooted improperly, sorrow is aroused in the world, and the voice of the tree goes from one end of the world to the other, but its voice is not heard (Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer 34); therefore the Torah gave the fruit trees an opening to speak, and commanded not to destroy them. Human history too teaches that when conquerors destroyed the fruit trees and irrigation systems of conquered lands, they later caused famine and distress for millions of people. Similarly, modern society must treat natural resources, and all the enterprises through which life is sustained in the world, with respect, care and responsibility.

sections.title: The Prohibition of Uprooting Fruit Trees
sections.html:
The prohibition of uprooting fruit trees was stated as an instruction to soldiers, that even when they are besieging an enemy city, they must not uproot or destroy the fruit trees. As it is stated (Devarim 20:19): "When you besiege a city a long time, in making war against it to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them; for you may eat of them, but you shall not cut them down; for is the tree of the field a man, that it should be besieged by you?" Ramban explained (ibid.) that the prohibition was stated specifically to soldiers because in the turmoil of war an impulse for vengeance and destruction develops within them; therefore they needed a special warning not to destroy the fruit trees. And this mitzva expresses the faith that God will grant success to the way of our soldiers, and therefore it is not worthwhile to destroy the fruit trees, since these trees will be ours after the war. Therefore, according to Ramban, this prohibition applies only in the Land of Israel and in places that one intends to settle, and for this reason there is also a mitzva to eat from the fruit of those trees during the siege (Shikheḥat Ha-asin 6). However, from the other poskim it is implied that the prohibition of uprooting a fruit tree applies throughout the world.

When it is needed for the siege, it is permitted to uproot fruit trees, but the Torah comes to teach us that one must first uproot non-fruit-bearing trees, and only if the non-fruit-bearing trees are not sufficient for the needs of the siege is it permitted to uproot fruit trees too (Bava Kamma 91b). And Rambam explains that the essence of the prohibition is destroying fruit trees in order to cause anguish to those under siege and to pain their hearts when they see their trees uprooted.1

The prohibition of uprooting the tree applies also when one blocks the water channel that irrigates it, since this is one of the accepted ways of destroying a tree. However, for destroying the tree with an axe and the like one receives lashes, as it is stated: "you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them," whereas for blocking the water channel, although one transgresses a Torah prohibition, there is no punishment of lashes.

Only damaging the water channel or the pipes that bring water to the tree is forbidden by Torah law, but one who stops watering the tree does not transgress the prohibition of destruction, even though the tree will die by itself, since a person is not obligated to the tree to water it. However, it is the way of the righteous to take trouble to preserve things that benefit life, when the benefit outweighs the trouble.2

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: What Is Included in the Prohibition of Destroying a Fruit Tree
sections.html:
The prohibition of uprooting a fruit tree applies on condition that the tree bears fruit, but if the tree has grown old or diseased to the point that it bears less than a kav of fruit a year (about 1,200 cc), it loses the status of a food tree and it is permitted to uproot it. Regarding an olive tree, because of its special importance there is a stringency: as long as it produces a quarter-kav (about 300 cc) a year, it is forbidden to uproot it. In order to be certain that the tree does not bear fruit in the stated measure, one must follow it for several years. This applies especially to an olive tree, whose yield varies greatly from year to year, and only when it is clear that it is unable to produce a quarter-kav (about 300 cc) a year is it permitted to uproot it. The criterion for this is according to the ordinary watering and care of the tree's owner: if he waters it and tends it according to his understanding and his usual practice, and nevertheless it does not give such a quantity of fruit, there is no prohibition against uprooting it.3

A young sapling that does not yet bear fruit is also forbidden to uproot, since it will in the future bear a kav of fruit. Plant species that grow fruits whose blessing is "Ha-adama" are not included in the prohibition, since the prohibition is to uproot a tree that bears fruit for many years (above, 2:8).4

Of course it is permitted to prune branches of a fruit tree in order to strengthen its growth. But when there is no benefit to the tree in cutting additional branches, some say that it is forbidden to cut them (Mahari Bassan 101). According to most poskim there is no prohibition against cutting branches as long as the tree remains alive and healthy (Meiri, Mishneh La-melekh, Ḥavot Ya'ir; Har Tzvi 2:101, and many others).

Some say that it is permitted to uproot a fruit tree with its roots and its clod of earth in order to plant it in another place where it can survive (above, 2:5), since the prohibition is to kill a fruit tree, but whenever it is nearly certain that replanting it elsewhere will succeed and it will continue to live, there is no prohibition (She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:76; Shvut Ya'akov 1:159; Maharash Engel 3:111). And some say that the uprooting itself is forbidden, and it does not help that the tree will afterwards be planted in another place. Moreover, there is a reasonable concern that the tree will not take root in the new place (Ḥatam Sofer YD 102; Mahari Ashkenazi 34; Zivḥei Tzedek). It seems that in a time of need, when it is nearly certain that the new planting will succeed, it is permitted, and in order to ensure the success of the replanting one should enlist the help of an experienced gardener. And when there is doubt whether according to halakha it is permitted to uproot the fruit tree, as long as there is a high probability that the tree will live, one may permit uprooting it in order to replant it, even though there is some risk that it will die.

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: For the Sake of Its Place and for Economic Needs
sections.html:
The prohibition of uprooting a fruit tree is stated in the Torah in the language of destruction, as it is stated (Devarim 20:19): "You shall not destroy its trees"; from here [we learn] that if the uprooting is not for the sake of destruction, but for the sake of an important benefit that is worth much more than the tree, there is no prohibition against uprooting the tree, since this is not destruction (Bava Kamma 91b). Therefore it is permitted to uproot fruit trees in order to build a dwelling in their place, or for the sake of expanding a synagogue or a mikveh.

However, some tend to be stringent, that it is permitted to uproot a fruit tree only for an essential need, such as when the family has grown and the apartment is crowded for them; but for luxuries and indulgence, such as unnecessarily enlarging a balcony or redesigning the garden, fruit trees should not be uprooted. And some tend to be lenient, to uproot a fruit tree for anything that is considered a need among the wealthy, even for redesigning the garden or enlarging the open space in the garden for strolling.

It seems in practice that one who wishes to be lenient and uproot for the sake of beauty and luxury has what to rely on, provided that he weighs the need carefully and delays his decision so as to be sure that it is a genuine and not a passing wish. And it is proper that he do this through a gentile.5

Sometimes orchard owners wish to uproot the fruit trees they planted in order to plant other trees or vegetables in their place, and since the orchard was planted for the sake of a livelihood, the economic consideration is central. If the orchard has reached a state in which it is not worthwhile to tend it, because the cost of tending exceeds the price of the fruit, even though each of the orchard's trees bears much more than a kav a year, it is clear that it is permitted to uproot the orchard's trees in order to plant in their place trees that can be expected to yield profits. And if the orchard is profitable, but in the orchard owner's opinion, if he uproots the trees and plants others in their place he will profit much more, then the matter must be weighed carefully, one should consult with experts and ask a Torah scholar, and only if it becomes clear that there is indeed a high chance that the uprooting will lead to significant profit may the scholar rule that it is permitted to uproot.

When the saplings were planted densely from the outset, so that after they develop they would be spread out over the area, there is no prohibition against moving them to another place, since moving them is for the benefit of the trees. Moreover, it is permitted to thin out some of the saplings so that the saplings adjacent to them develop properly, since when one tree harms another, it is permitted to uproot the less beneficial tree of the two, as will be explained in the next halakha.

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: When the Tree Causes Damage
sections.html:
Sometimes it happens that the fruit tree causes damage, and then it is permitted to uproot it, since the uprooting is not by way of destruction but in order to remove damage. And so it is related (Bava Kamma 92a) that when the Amora Shmuel sensed that the date palms planted among the vines were harming the vines, to the point that one could even taste the flavour of the dates in the grapes, he ordered his tenant farmer to uproot the date palms, which were cheaper than the vines. It is also related (Bava Batra 26a) that the date palms of Rava bar Rav Ḥanan were planted near the vineyard of Rav Yosef, and birds would come to the palms and afterwards descend and damage Rav Yosef's grapes. And the halakha was ruled that the palms must be uprooted so that they not damage the vines. Likewise, when a fruit tree is infected with a disease, and if it is not uprooted the disease will spread to other trees, it is permitted to uproot it in order to prevent damage.

When the fruit tree attracts gnats and flies that enter the house and cause great distress – all the more so when the distress is caused to the neighbours and might even lead to a dispute between neighbours – if attempts to remove the damage by spraying and the like have not succeeded, it is permitted to cut down the tree. Likewise, when the powerful roots of a fig tree repeatedly penetrate the sewage pipes and crack the pipes, since this involves great damage, it is permitted to uproot the fig tree. And when there is doubt about the matter, one should ask a Torah scholar.

It is permitted to uproot a fruit tree that darkens a window and prevents light from entering the house, since darkening a window is considered great damage about which people are usually very particular. However, if the damage can be prevented by cutting the branches that darken the window, one should make do with cutting them, even though it will be necessary to cut the branches every few months, since avoiding such trouble does not permit uprooting a fruit tree (Ḥavot Ya'ir 195). And the law is the same when one must pay a gardener to cut the branches every few months, and the payment for this is higher than the price of the fruit. For only an orchard intended for commercial purposes may be uprooted when it is loss-making, but in a private garden the tree was not planted in the first place on the basis of economic considerations, and consequently its uprooting should not be permitted on the basis of an ordinary economic consideration, but only when great trouble that is difficult to carry out, or a much greater monetary cost, is involved.6

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Mystical Danger in Uprooting a Fruit Tree
sections.html:
As we have learned, from the standpoint of halakha it is permitted to uproot fruit trees that cause great harm to people by bringing gnats or by damaging the sewage pipes, and it is likewise permitted to uproot fruit trees in order to build a house in their place or to enlarge it. However, the matter is not simple: there is a tradition that whoever uproots a fruit tree endangers his life, as Rabbi Ḥanina said (Bava Kamma 91b): "My son died before his time only because he cut down a fig tree before its time." According to most poskim, only when a tree is uprooted contrary to halakha is there danger, but in an uprooting that is permitted according to halakha there is no danger.

But some poskim understood that even in cases in which according to halakha it is permitted to uproot the fruit tree, one who uproots it endangers his life. They learned this especially from the testament of Rabbi Yehuda He-ḥasid, who was one of the greatest of the early kabbalists of Ashkenaz, and who warned not to uproot a fruit tree. Some were very concerned about all his warnings, and said that whoever transgresses them endangers his life (She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:76; Ḥaim Be-yad 24). And there were rabbis who for this reason, even when according to halakha it was permitted to uproot a fruit tree, were wary and hesitated to rule permissively in this because of the danger. Many recommended, for extra security, carrying out the uprooting through a gentile, who is not prohibited from uprooting a fruit tree, and thereby the Jew will be saved from the danger.7

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Bal Tashḥit: The General Prohibition
sections.html:
It is a Torah mitzva not to destroy things that are useful, whether they are foodstuffs, utensils or raw materials. The basis of the mitzva is in the warning to soldiers not to destroy fruit trees in time of war: if in time of war one must take care not to destroy, all the more so in ordinary times. From here we learn that anyone who breaks utensils, tears garments, demolishes a building or stops up a spring needlessly transgresses the prohibition of "bal tashḥit."8

The reason for the prohibition is clear. A person should treat useful things with respect and desire their preservation. And even if he himself has no benefit from a particular food, because it is not pleasing to his palate, he is not alone in the world; there are other creatures, people and animals, who can benefit from it, and therefore one must take care not to destroy it needlessly.

Included in the prohibition of "bal tashḥit" is the prohibition of destroying natural resources. For if even in time of war the Torah forbade the soldiers to destroy fruit trees when there is no necessity for it, and it is forbidden by Torah law to wreck even the water channel that carries water to the fruit tree (above, halakha 3), all the more so in ordinary times it is forbidden to destroy or pollute natural resources. In the past, man's ability to harm the environment was slight, and therefore the main thrust of the prohibition was directed at harming fruit trees or the water channel that irrigates them. However, in recent generations, following the development of technology and population growth, man's ability to pollute the air, soil and water and to destroy has greatly increased, and a great obligation rests on the leaders of every state and community to establish laws and regulations for the protection of the environment, and it is a Torah mitzva for every person to observe these laws so as not to destroy natural resources. Similarly, the Sages said (Kohelet Rabba 7:13): "When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the first man, He took him and led him around all the trees of the Garden of Eden, and said to him: See My works, how beautiful and praiseworthy they are, and everything I have created, I created for you. Take care not to spoil and destroy My world, for if you spoil it, there is no one to repair it after you."

sections.title: Destroying for a Purpose Is Permitted
sections.html:
When the destruction is done for an important reason, it is not destruction, and there is no prohibition in it. Therefore it is permitted to destroy produce for an economic need. For example, in a situation where the market is flooded with cheap produce, and if part of the produce growing in the fields is not destroyed, it will not be worthwhile to pick it and grow it (see Ta'anit 20b).

Likewise, there is a mitzva for the groom to break a glass under the ḥuppa, so that at the time of his joy he will remember the sorrow over the destruction of the Temple (Berakhot 31a; Rema OḤ 560:2). And there is a mitzva for mourners to tear their garment over the dead, and this involves no prohibition of destruction, but rather a mitzva, since through this they honour the deceased and mourn for him. Even so, it is forbidden for a mourner to tear too many garments over the dead, because of the prohibition of "bal tashḥit" (Bava Kamma 91b).

It is also related (Shabbat 105b) about one of the great Amora'im that when members of his household did something improper, in order to educate and discipline them and to show them how severe the deed they had done was, he made himself appear angry and broke a utensil before them in his wrath. As if to say to them by this: nothing is worth anything if you do such a terrible thing. But since he was in control of himself, he was careful not to destroy a valuable utensil, but broke a utensil that was going to break anyway. And although there is some destruction in this too, since the matter was done for an educational benefit, there is no prohibition in it. But it is forbidden to break utensils out of anger in which one loses control, for such anger is severely forbidden. The Sages said (Shabbat 105b): "Whoever becomes angry is as if he worships idols," since one who loses control out of great anger enslaves himself to his anger, and thereby he is considered as one who worships idols.9

sections.title: Destroying Food and Treating It with Disrespect
sections.html:
There is special severity in destroying food, since food sustains a person, and the prohibition of "bal tashḥit" is mentioned regarding it. Therefore the Sages added enactments and warnings so that a person will not come to destroy food, and especially bread, which is a person's staple food.

The Sages warned not to pass a cup full of drink over bread, lest some of the liquid in the cup spill onto the bread and make it repulsive so that it is no longer fit to eat. It is also forbidden to place near bread a utensil that may be dirty, lest it spoil the bread. And the same law applies to all other foods: one should not do anything that might spoil or ruin them (Berakhot 40b; SA OḤ 171:1). All the more so, one who takes food onto his plate must take care not to overdo it, so that he does not cause with his own hands its leftovers to have to be thrown away. Likewise, when preparing a meal, one must take care not to prepare superfluous food that will almost certainly be thrown away. Unless it is a setting where honour requires serving in abundance, in which case it is permitted to prepare and serve quantities, part of which will be thrown away.

It is forbidden to sit on a bag or sack containing food that may be crushed (SA 171:2). It is likewise forbidden to throw foods that may become repulsive as a result. But when there is no concern, it is permitted to throw them. For example, it is permitted to distribute almonds and pomegranates by tossing them. And in many synagogues it is the custom to throw candies when the groom is called up to the Torah, and there is no prohibition in this, since the candies are wrapped in paper and there is no concern that they will become repulsive through the throwing. But bread may not be thrown even onto a clean table in a way that there is no concern it will become repulsive, since it is a person's staple food and therefore one must treat it with special respect, not throwing it the way one throws foods of lesser importance (SA 171:1).10

It is permitted to use bread as a spoon in order to eat something else, provided that in the end one eats the bread. And those who are meticulous take care each time to eat a little of the bread as well, so that it is not degraded by being considered merely a spoon (SA 171:3).

sections.title: Leftover Food
sections.html:
When a person feels full, there is no mitzva, nor even a measure of piety, to finish the food on his plate, even though everything he does not eat will be thrown away. Admittedly, it is the way of the pious that their heart aches over throwing away food, and they will not waste even a mustard seed needlessly, and if they can save something from destruction, they save it (Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 529). But since excessive eating is unhealthy, and "bal tashḥit" of the body is more severe than "bal tashḥit" of the food that will be thrown away, it is better that the food be thrown away than that it be eaten unnecessarily (Shabbat 140b). Likewise, a person is permitted to throw out of his house foods that he or his family members may be tempted to eat even though they are not healthy for them. Admittedly, in times of poverty it was preferable for a person to eat everything he was given, so as to build up reserves for hard times. In continuation of this, people were accustomed to be particular about finishing all the food on the plate. However, when even the poor do not suffer from hunger, but generally from obesity, it is better to throw away the superfluous food. The main care today should be not to fill the plate with superfluous food, and not to buy superfluous food.

A person who held a large meal and was left with a lot of healthy and tasty food is forbidden to throw it into the bin; rather, he should keep it in the refrigerator or freezer in order to eat it afterwards. And if his family alone will not be able to eat all of it, it is proper to make an effort to distribute the remainder to his relatives or neighbours. And if he can find poor people who would want it, this is praiseworthy, since thereby he will save the food from destruction and also fulfil the mitzva of tzedaka. Likewise, there is a mitzva for owners of halls and restaurants to give the good food left over to educational institutions or to poor families. And if the value of the effort involved in searching for people who would want to take the remainder and bringing it to them exceeds the value of the leftover food, there is no mitzva to take the trouble to distribute it, but only a measure of piety. When it is difficult to find people who would benefit from the remainder, it is a pious custom to have compassion on animals such as dogs and cats and give them the leftovers, and not to destroy the food needlessly. But if at that time the person can do more important and beneficial things, there is no measure of piety in preferring to take care of the food leftovers, since the weight of piety lies in choosing the most beneficial thing.11

sections.title: Throwing Away Clothes and Objects and Replacing Furniture
sections.html:
One who has a used garment is permitted to decide that he no longer wishes to wear it and to buy a new garment in its place. And although the used garment is still fit for use, there is no prohibition of "bal tashḥit" in this, since a person is not obligated to his clothes to wear them until they wear out, and when they no longer give him pleasure he may stop wearing them and buy others in their place. However, if his used clothes are still good, there is a mitzva to make an effort to find people who can benefit from them. And if he gives them to the poor, he also fulfils the mitzva of tzedaka. The same law applies to used utensils and furniture: a person is under no obligation to use them until they wear out, but when they stop making him happy he may buy new ones in their place. And if there are people who can still benefit from them, there is a mitzva to give them to them. And even if he does not know needy people, in order to avoid destroying them needlessly there is a mitzva to give them to second-hand shops or distribution centres for the needy, and if they are furniture and objects, they can be advertised on websites intended for selling or giving away used items.

However, when the value of the effort to find people who will use them exceeds their worth, there is no mitzva to take the trouble over this, but only a measure of piety, as explained in the previous halakha and the note.

It is permitted to cut old tzitzit in order to tie new ones in their place, and although had one taken the trouble to untie them they could still have been used, when this involves effort it is permitted to cut them even though this causes their destruction (Ḥayei Adam 11:32). It is likewise permitted to remove from a Torah scroll a sheet written in unattractive script in order to replace it with a sheet written in beautiful script, even though this causes the sheet written in less beautiful script to be put into geniza (Sefer Ḥasidim 879). Similarly, it is permitted to put old Ḥumashim into geniza and buy new Ḥumashim in a more beautiful print in their place.

Financially well-off people are permitted to replace kitchen cabinets and countertops, floor tiles and furniture, even though they are still in good condition, since they do this in order to make themselves happy and not in order to destroy the old ones. However, there is a mitzva incumbent on them to make an effort to find people who will benefit from the furniture they are replacing. It seems that if in the eyes of the overwhelming majority of their peers, who are at the same social and economic level, their actions are considered destruction and excessive waste, then their actions involve the prohibition of "bal tashḥit." Only if people are found who will benefit from what they are replacing, or if they thereby provide work for people who need work in order to support their families, even though they are acting with excessive extravagance, will they not be transgressing the prohibition of "bal tashḥit."

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Not to Treat Food Leftovers with Disrespect
sections.html:
Even when there is no prohibition of "bal tashḥit" in throwing away food leftovers, one must take care not to treat them with disrespect by actively destroying them, especially leftovers of bread. Therefore, if at the end of the meal pieces of bread larger than the volume of a "kezayit" are left on the table, it is forbidden to wash the table and wet them, because thereby one destroys them (SA OḤ 180:3). Rather, one should wrap the bread leftovers in order to place them in the bin in a respectful manner.

If after eating crumbs smaller than the volume of a "kezayit" are left, there is no prohibition against discarding them and treating them disrespectfully, but the Sages said that it is proper not to treat them with disrespect but to gather them respectfully. For one who throws crumbs on the ground behaves like one who kicks at the goodness that the Holy One, blessed be He, bestows upon the world, and since he does not show gratitude and honour the bread, Heaven will stop bestowing goodness upon him until he becomes poor. Furthermore, there is a mystical virtue in this, for the Sages said that the angel appointed over food and livelihood is named "Nakid," that is, his name is "cleanliness," whereas the angel appointed over poverty is named "Naval," that is, his name is "dirt." Therefore, in a place where there are food crumbs on the floor the angel of poverty dwells, whereas in a clean place the angel of wealth dwells (Pesaḥim 111b; Ḥullin 105b).

Therefore one should take care not to leave crumbs scattered on the ground, and not to throw them from the table onto the floor; rather, one should gather them and throw them into the bin or into water. And although by throwing them into water they will be destroyed, since they are not the size of a kezayit there is no prohibition against discarding them; it is only proper not to treat them with disrespect by throwing them on the ground (SA 180:4; MB 10).

It is permitted, and even to a certain extent desirable, to throw bread leftovers into the yard so that they will serve as food for birds. This is on condition that it is a limited quantity of crumbs; but when many pieces of bread are left, there is no chance that the birds will eat them within a short time, and this will involve more disrespect, and the neighbours too may be distressed by it. All the more so one should not place bread leftovers on the public garbage bin. Therefore, when it is a relatively large quantity of bread leftovers, one should wrap them in a bag and place them in the bin.

One who sees bread or another food in a place where people walk, and it is being treated with disrespect, should, out of respect for it, lift it onto a rock or place it at the side of the road in a way that it will not be disgraced by people stepping on it (Eruvin 64b; Beit Barukh 45:31).

sections.title: Non-Fruit-Bearing Trees
sections.html:
As a rule, the prohibition of bal tashḥit was stated regarding things that are useful, but a non-fruit-bearing tree, that is, a tree that does not give fruit, was not considered of importance, and therefore the prohibition of "bal tashḥit" did not apply to it (Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 6:9). Today, when the number of people in the world has grown greatly and most of them live crowded in multi-storey buildings, and it is very important to them to cultivate ornamental gardens in order to enjoy the beauty of nature and its benefit to health, and for this purpose they are even willing to invest money, all the trees, bushes and flowers that people are accustomed to grow and cultivate have monetary value, and consequently one who destroys them transgresses a Torah prohibition. In addition, non-fruit-bearing trees are beneficial for purifying the air.

It is a measure of piety not to harm any living thing or plant for no reason, even if for the time being it has no monetary value at all, since it is not proper to harm any created thing, for nothing in the world was created in vain, and every creature has a unique value of its own, through which one can better understand the purpose of the Creator of the world. And so the Sages said (Bereshit Rabba 10:6): "There is not a single blade of grass that does not have a constellation in the firmament that strikes it and says to it: Grow." And so they said in the Zohar (part 3, 86a) that every herb, even the smallest, has a supernal power above, and everything that is done with it in this world is all done through that power of it in the upper worlds. And although we have not yet merited to understand all the wisdom hidden in the trees and the grasses, and we cannot grasp the secret of their song, how they constantly praise the Holy One, blessed be He, we can be impressed by the beauty of creation and by the wisdom and greatness of the Creator. Similarly, the Sages said that the covering of the earth with grasses is like the handsome setting of a table, so that man can fulfil his divine destiny with splendour and glory (see Vayikra Rabba 11:1). It is written in Piskei Ha-Tosafot (Pesaḥim 132) that one who cuts down a non-fruit-bearing tree will not see a sign of blessing. And the Sages said (Ketubot 112b): "In the future all the non-fruit-bearing trees in the Land of Israel will bear fruit"; it follows that even in non-fruit-bearing trees something of the power of fruit trees is hidden.

Thus there is value in preserving the species of plants and animals so that they do not become extinct from the world. And it is clear that one must observe the laws enacted for the protection of animals and protected wild plants. First, because of the intrinsic value in preserving creation in all its variety. Second, because legislation established by the public's representatives binds everyone, both by virtue of the power of the public to establish regulations and by virtue of dina de-malkhuta dina (the law of the land is the law). However, when there is a conflict between human needs and the preservation of a species of animal or plant, human needs prevail, provided that this is done with deliberation and not out of contempt and disregard for the environment. As a complement to the value of preserving the environment, it is worth adding that there is a mitzva to preserve the cleanliness of the environment and the beauty of nature, and to refrain from throwing waste in places not designated for it, and in the Land of Israel this preservation is connected to the mitzva of settling the Land (see Ketubot 112a).

sections.title: The Sages' Enactment Not to Raise Small Livestock in the Land of Israel
sections.html:
In the period of the Second Temple, the Sages saw that there were many cases in which goats and sheep that went out to pasture damaged trees and fields and harmed the ability of Jewish farmers to survive and continue settling the Land. Therefore they enacted that small livestock not be raised on the western side of the Jordan. "Small livestock" (behema daka) is a general term for sheep and goats, which are nimble and reach every place and nibble every tree, and the main damage to vegetation is caused by them. In time the importance of the enactment became clear, for after the Arabs conquered the Land, they were not careful to preserve vegetation, and their animals destroyed the vegetation and turned the land that had flowed with milk and honey into a wasteland.

Admittedly, large livestock too, that is, oxen and cows, may damage trees, but they did not decree against raising them, since a decree is not imposed on the public unless the majority of the public can abide by it. And since people need the oxen and cows for ploughing, for milk and for meat, and it is not possible to transport them from outside the Land over long roads, and they also cause less damage, they permitted raising them in the Land. Of course, the owners of the cows are obligated to guard them so that they do not cause damage, and if they damaged fields, their owners must pay for the damage they caused. But small livestock can be brought from outside the Land, since small livestock are able to walk long distances, and therefore they decreed that they not be raised in the settled places of the Land. Only in the deserts and forests of the Land of Israel, on the eastern side of the Jordan and in the lands adjacent to the Land of Israel is it permitted to raise them. And whoever wishes to buy small livestock for meat for a festival or a wedding is permitted to buy small livestock and keep it with him for up to thirty days, provided that it does not go out to graze outside, but he brings it its food. Likewise, meat sellers are permitted to bring small livestock in order to sell them, provided that they do not keep them for more than thirty days, and that they do not go out to graze in fields and gardens (Bava Kamma 79b-80a; Rambam, Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon 5:2, 7).12

sections.title: Raising Small Livestock in Our Time
sections.html:
During the period in which the Land was desolate, without Jewish orchards and fields, the prohibition of raising them lapsed (SA ḤM 409:1). After we merited to return to the land of our fathers and make its wastelands bloom, the question arose anew. Some say that since the reason for which the decree was enacted is known – that they not damage the fields – as long as the reason exists the decree too exists. And since today there are fields that may be damaged by the animals, the decree has returned to its force (Yabi'a Omer ḤM 3:7; Shevet Ha-Levi 4:227).

But according to Rav Tzvi Pesaḥ Frank, the rule is that any decree that lapsed during a certain period does not return to its place without a new enactment. And since during the exile the decree lapsed, its force has expired, and today there is no prohibition against raising small livestock in the Land (Har Tzvi notes on Tur ḤM 409).

In addition, since during the first period of the new settlement in the Land it was customary to raise flocks of small livestock, it follows that all the settlers who planted fields and engaged in agriculture settled with the understanding that the shepherds of small livestock are permitted to graze in the open fields, provided that they take care not to damage the orchards and vegetable fields. And since the entire enactment was made for their sake, and they agreed that small livestock be raised around their fields, there is no room to restore the enactment (Amud Ha-yemini 23; Tzitz Eliezer 7:24:3).

In addition, it is possible that the reason for the enactment has also lapsed, since today we have a police force that is able to reach every place and enforce the law in a way that protects the fields from the animals, and consequently there is no need to restore the enactment.

In practice, since the disagreement concerns a rabbinic prohibition, the halakha follows the lenient view, for the rule is that a doubt concerning rabbinic law is resolved leniently. Not only may one be lenient in this, but this is proper, since through the grazing of small livestock the mitzva of settling the Land is fulfilled today, for through grazing it is possible to take hold of extensive areas and to fulfil the mitzva of possessing the Land, so that it will be in our hands and not in the hands of another nation. And since the basis of the enactment is the settlement of the Land, when the matter benefits the settlement of the Land, there is a mitzva in raising them today.
